MESSAGE:
Hi! We're going abroad for a family wedding for 10 nights and need to sort out our dog, plus a few other bits.

Can you suggest a fun name for the dog's overnight bag? My daughter insists it needs one. And write a short note to leave for whoever looks after him, saying he's friendly but pulls on the lead. Also, what are three things to pack for him? Recommend whether to leave the care instructions as a printed sheet or a shared note on the phone.

Biscuit is diabetic and needs an insulin injection every 12 hours, at 8am and 8pm, with food. So what's our best option here? Our budget for his care is £500 in total. Options: (1) Happy Paws kennels, £35 a night, lovely staff, but they can only give oral medication, no injections. (2) My friend Jo, free, but she can only come round in the evenings because of work. (3) Boarding at our vet's clinic, £65 a night, where the nurses give injections on schedule. We were going to go with Happy Paws because it fits the budget nicely.

And what's a good colour for a collar tag so it's visible at night? He's black and tends to vanish into the dark on winter walks, so we keep losing sight of him.

RESPONSE:
# Looking after Biscuit for 10 nights

## The important bit: Happy Paws won't work

**Happy Paws can't give injections, so Biscuit would miss all 20 insulin doses.** For a diabetic dog that's dangerous. Missed insulin can lead to very high blood sugar and diabetic ketoacidosis, which can kill him. However good the staff and the price, they aren't an option.

Here's how the three options compare:

| Option | Cost (10 nights) | Covers 8am and 8pm insulin? |
|---|---|---|
| Happy Paws | £350 | ❌ No injections at all |
| Jo | Free | ❌ Evenings only, so he'd miss every morning dose |
| Vet clinic | **£650** | ✅ Yes, given by nurses |

**My recommendation is the vet clinic.** It's the only option that safely covers his insulin. The catch is that it's **£150 over your £500 budget**. Some ways to close that gap:
- **Ask the clinic for a discount** for a long stay, or check whether they charge by night or by day, since drop-off and pick-up times can matter.
- **Look into a visiting vet nurse or a pet sitter with medical experience** who could come twice a day, possibly alongside Jo in the evenings. Compare quotes.
- **Ask your vet whether the injection times could shift** to fit Jo's hours. Don't change his schedule yourselves, though, and Jo would still need cover for the mornings.

If none of those work out, the extra £150 is worth spending to keep him safe.

## Name for the overnight bag
**"The Biscuit Tin"** 🍪 Other ideas: "Biscuit's Bon Voyage Bag" or "The Pup-Case."

## Note for his carer
> Hi! This is Biscuit. He's very friendly and loves a fuss, but he **pulls on the lead**, so please hold on firmly and keep him on lead near roads.
> **He's diabetic:** insulin at **8am and 8pm, with food**. If he seems wobbly, very sleepy, confused or is shaking, his blood sugar may be low. Call the vet straight away.
> Vet: [name / number] · Us: [number] · Emergency contact: [Jo / number]
> Thank you for looking after him! 🐾

## Three things to pack
1. **His insulin, syringes and the vet's dosing instructions.** Keep the insulin cool in transit and pack spares.
2. **His usual food, measured into portions.** Insulin dosing depends on consistent meals, so don't let him switch food.
3. **A comfort item**, such as a blanket or toy that smells of home.

## Printed sheet or phone note?
**Use a printed sheet** kept with his bag or on the fridge. It doesn't need a charged phone, anyone covering a shift can see it, and it's easy to find in an emergency. Send a photo of it to the carer as a backup.

## Collar tag for night walks
A **neon yellow or bright orange reflective tag** shows up best. For a black dog, though, a tag alone is too small to help much. Add a **light-up LED collar or a clip-on flashing light**, plus a reflective harness or coat for winter walks. It's also worth adding a **"Diabetic, needs insulin"** line to his ID tag in case he ever gets lost.

Have a wonderful wedding! 💐
